newsitem.title: USA: Medicare heats up as Congress works on budget bill.
newsitem.headline: Medicare heats up as Congress works on budget bill.

text.p: The Medicare wars flared up Friday as Congress and the White House sparred over plans to to make affluent seniors pay more for doctor's care and raise the program's eligibility age to 67 from the current 65.
The Senate's top Republican rejected parts of a White House compromise proposal on so-called Medicare affluence testing, calling it a "poison pill" that could doom the plan.
Earlier Friday, White House chief of staff Erskine Bowles told House Democrats that President Clinton would not agree to the Senate-passed plan to raise the Medicare eligibility age.
Democratic aides said Bowles assured lawmakers, to much applause, that Clinton would veto a budget bill that did not meet his priorities.
Senior citizens' groups entered the fray launching a lobbying campaign to defeat the Medicare measures, charging they undermined the health programme for 38 million Americans.

"Older people want a balanced budget. They're willing to make sacrifices for their children's and grandchildren's futures. But these proposals go way too far, are bad public policy and just don't make sense," said Howard Bedlin of the National Council on the Ageing.
The action came as lawmakers worked on compromise legislation to balance the budget in five years. Congressional leaders hope to complete work on a final plan by Aug. 1.
The Senate version of the budget bill would make seniors with incomes of $50,000 or more and couples making $75,000 and above pay higher monthly Medicare premiums.
Clinton originally did not want the proposal included in the budget, saying it should be debated instead as part of long-term Medicare reform.

The president has shifted, with aides saying he might support such a policy if changes were made. Among revisions, the White House wants higher payments collected by the Treasury Department, not the Department of Health and Human Services.

"I think that's a potential problem. I think that's kind of a poison pill and turns it into a tax, which is not our goal, not our desire," Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott said emerging from a meeting on the Medicare.

The administration says using HHS would be unwieldy and expensive. The White House also wants to cap the premium even for the most affluent, fearing that without such a change many seniors might decide to leave Medicare altogether.
The government now subsidises 75 percent of the Medicare Part B premium, beneficiaries pay 25 percent. The premium would be $540 next year when the legislation took effect.
Under the Senate bill the premium would rise to a maximum of $2,160 for couples making $125,000 and individuals making more than $100,000. The House did not include the means test.
Supporters said Congress cannot put off tough action to ensure the long-term solvency of Medicare. The financial outlook is dire in the next centuray as baby boomers retire.

House Democratic Leader Dick Gephardt, at a news conference with senior citizens' groups, accused Republicans of trying to undermine Medicare. But Senate support for the afluence test and other changes was bipartisan.
Further, House Republicans are holding back waiting for political cover from Clinton.
The White House refuses to bend on increasing the eligibility age, another provision approved by the Senate.
After meeting privately with Democrats, Bowles said he did not see how the change "makes any sense whatsoever" charging it could increase the ranks of the uninsured.

The House Thursday voted 414-14 to oppose the plan. A coalition of moderate Senate Democrats and Republicans Friday vowed to continue fighting for the age increase. Nevada Democratic Sen. Richard Bryan told opponents of the Medicare changes to get a "vertebrae transplant."
